One four-stroke cycle spans two crankshaft revolutions. The intake valve admits air, both valves close for compression and power, and the exhaust valve opens to release spent gas. A spark initiates combustion in a petrol engine.
Combustion pressure drives the piston down and turns the crankshaft.
The piston descends. An open intake valve lets fresh air enter.
The piston rises while an open exhaust valve releases spent gas.

The connecting rod transfers piston force to a crank journal, producing rotation.

Understand the two sides of a turbocharger.

Exhaust gas drives a turbine. A shared shaft turns a compressor that supplies compressed intake air. The intake and exhaust streams stay separate. A turbocharger can increase the air mass available for combustion.
Compression heats air. A charge-air cooler removes some of that heat before the air reaches the cylinders. A wastegate can bypass exhaust around the turbine to help control boost.

Explore speed, torque and gear ratios.

A transmission changes the relationship between engine speed and wheel speed. A low gear delivers more wheel torque for a given engine torque. A higher gear lets the car travel faster at the same engine speed.

In an ideal reduction, output speed equals input speed divided by the ratio, while output torque is multiplied by that ratio. Real gears have losses. The final drive adds another ratio between the transmission and wheels.

Manual gearboxes use a clutch to connect the engine. Many conventional automatics use a fluid torque converter, often with a lock-up clutch to reduce slip. Dual-clutch transmissions use a different arrangement. The ratios below are teaching examples, not BMW transmission specifications.

An engine family code is a more precise clue than a boot badge. BMW identifies the N55 as a turbocharged inline six, and the S63 family underpins the V8 in the F10 M5. A car model badge alone is not a complete engine identification.

Family names such as N55 and B58 cover multiple versions and applications. Production date, market and the complete engine designation matter. Look up a documented example instead of assuming every digit follows one universal rule.

An engine family is not a parts-compatibility guarantee. Changes within a family may alter cooling, fueling, control software or packaging. Use the full vehicle identification and official model documentation when establishing an exact variant.

Coolant absorbs heat from the engine and carries it to a radiator. Air flowing through the radiator takes heat away. A pump circulates coolant, and a thermostat helps the engine reach and maintain its operating temperature.

The engine sits behind the cabin and drives the rear wheels through a five-speed manual gearbox. This entry describes the road car, whose output differs from Procar racing versions.
The original M supercar. A mid-mounted straight-six.
The road-going M1 pairs a 3,453 cm³ six-cylinder with a mid-engine layout. Its M88 uses four valves per cylinder, individual intake throttles and dry-sump lubrication.
A six-speed manual gearbox sends torque to the rear axle through an M differential lock. Its compact body brought M engineering into the first-generation 1 Series Coupé.
Compact dimensions. Twin turbos. Six-speed manual.
The compact M car, powered by the twin-turbo S55.
The M2 Competition uses the S55 3.0-litre six-cylinder with two turbochargers, replacing the original M2’s N55 engine. Its cooling and oil supply are adapted for demanding driving.
The rear-drive layout is paired with a standard six-speed manual gearbox or an optional seven-speed M dual-clutch transmission. An Active M Differential manages rear-axle locking.
A new generation of compact, rear-driven M performance.
The engine drives the rear wheels through an eight-speed M Steptronic transmission or optional six-speed manual. An electronically controlled Active M Differential supports traction.
The first M3’s 2,302 cm³ S14 has four cylinders and four valves per cylinder. Its compact, naturally aspirated design reflects the car’s touring-car homologation origins.
The four-cylinder origin of an M legend.
A five-speed manual transmission sends torque to the rear wheels. The later European 3.2-litre model added Double VANOS and different power and torque ratings.
The European 3.0-litre M3 uses the naturally aspirated S50B30 with individual throttles and VANOS inlet-camshaft adjustment. This is distinct from the lower-output North American powertrain.
510 PS. Twin-turbo six. An unmistakable silhouette.
This entry is the rear-wheel-drive Competition Coupé with an eight-speed M Steptronic transmission. M xDrive versions and later facelifts are separate factory specifications.
Two mono-scroll turbochargers supply the 3.0-litre S58 six-cylinder. A dedicated cooling system and M-specific oil supply support sustained high-load use.
A five-speed manual gearbox and rear-wheel drive complete the original M5 formula. The North American S38-powered model has a different factory output.
The first M5 adapts the M1-derived, 3,453 cm³ six-cylinder to a four-door sedan. The European M88/3 uses natural aspiration and a four-valve cylinder head.
The first M5. Motorsport engineering in a discreet sedan.
A hand-built six-cylinder chapter in M5 history.
The front-mounted engine drives the rear wheels through a five-speed manual gearbox. The E34 continued the M5’s restrained sedan profile while improving its performance.
2024 launch specification · combined hybrid system figures
727 PS and 1,000 Nm combined. The plug-in hybrid M5.
An eight-speed M Steptronic transmission and M xDrive distribute the hybrid system’s drive torque. A rechargeable high-voltage battery also enables electric-only driving.

The petrol engine and electric motor reach their peaks at different operating points. Combined system output is the factory-rated capability of the coordinated drivetrain, not the sum of both individual peak ratings. The engine sound mode illustrates the V8 only.
The front-mounted straight-six works with a five-speed manual gearbox and rear-wheel drive. The related North American M6 used a different engine specification.
The M635CSi gives the E24 luxury coupé a 3,453 cm³ M88 six-cylinder with twin overhead camshafts and 24 valves. These figures describe the non-catalyst European version.
The sharknose grand tourer with an M88 heart.
A carbon roof above. A naturally aspirated V10 ahead.
At launch, a seven-speed SMG automated manual transmission delivered torque to the rear axle. The roof uses carbon-fibre-reinforced plastic to reduce mass high in the body.

The E63 M6 uses a 5.0-litre S85 V10 with individual throttles. Its naturally aspirated powertrain makes peak power high in the rev range and brings a very different character from later turbocharged M6 models.
A seven-speed M dual-clutch transmission and Active M Differential deliver drive to the rear wheels. Competition Package versions have different power ratings.
The F13 M6 replaces the previous generation’s V10 with a 4.4-litre twin-turbo V8. The engine combines direct injection, Valvetronic and turbochargers packaged within the cylinder banks.
The M6 moves to a twin-turbo V8.
625 PS. M xDrive. Grand touring with an M edge.
A 4.4-litre V8 with two turbochargers supplies the M8 Competition. The compressors sit inside the V, while separate cooling circuits manage engine and charge-air temperatures.
The eight-speed M Steptronic transmission, M xDrive and Active M Differential work together to deliver the V8’s torque. This is the two-door Competition Coupé, rather than the Gran Coupé.
A five-speed manual transmission sends power to the rear wheels. A long bonnet, rearward seating position and compact two-seat body define this open-top M model.
A small roadster. A full-strength European M straight-six.
The early European M Roadster uses the 3,201 cm³ S50B32 straight-six from the contemporary M3. Its 321 PS specification differs from both the early US S52 version and the later S54 model.
Six cylinders, six manual gears and an open sky.
The Z4 M Roadster combines the 3,246 cm³ S54 six-cylinder with natural aspiration and an 8,000 rpm engine-speed ceiling. It shares its engine family with the E46 M3.
An eight-speed M Steptronic gearbox, rear-biased M xDrive and an Active M Differential bring the M powertrain to the X3’s taller, five-door body.
S58 power arrives in the X3.
M xDrive, an Active M Differential and an eight-speed M Steptronic transmission deliver drive beneath the X4’s sloping roofline. Later model-year torque ratings differ.
The X4 M Competition shares its twin-turbo 3.0-litre S58 with the X3 M Competition. This entry records the original 510 PS and 600 Nm factory specification.
The X4 silhouette, backed by a 510 PS M straight-six.
2020 European launch specification · before mild hybrid
An eight-speed M Steptronic gearbox, M xDrive and an Active M Differential send drive to the wheels. The 2023 facelift introduced a different engine generation with 48-volt assistance.
The original F95 Competition uses a twin-turbo 4.4-litre S63 V8. Its 625 PS output is delivered with M-specific cooling, chassis tuning and an all-wheel-drive system.
The X5, with 625 PS of twin-turbo M V8 power.

A dramatic roofline and a twin-turbo M V8.
The eight-speed M Steptronic transmission, M xDrive and Active M Differential are paired with the X6’s coupé-like SUV body. Later S68 mild-hybrid models are different specifications.
The pre-facelift F96 X6 M Competition has a 4.4-litre S63 twin-turbo V8. Its 625 PS and 750 Nm match the corresponding X5 M Competition launch specification.

653 PS combined. V8 power meets a rechargeable battery.

The hybrid drive system sends power through M xDrive. Electric assistance and electric-only operation distinguish this model from a conventional V8 SUV.
An eight-speed Steptronic Sport transmission and a front-axle Torsen limited-slip differential work with xDrive. M135i is an M Performance model within the 1 Series.
The F40 M135i uses a transversely mounted 2.0-litre four-cylinder turbo engine. Its layout and all-wheel-drive system mark a new direction for the 1 Series performance hatchback.
A compact, rear-driven coupé with a turbocharged four.
An eight-speed Sport automatic transmission sends drive to the rear axle. This entry describes the 230i, rather than the six-cylinder M240i or the separate M2.
The G42 230i’s 2.0-litre four-cylinder turbo engine produces 255 US horsepower and 295 lb-ft. This compact coupé keeps a longitudinal powertrain and rear-wheel-drive architecture.
2021 US launch specification · 294 lb-ft in BMW release
A low-slung two-door interpretation of the 4 Series.
The 2021 US launch release rates the G22 430i’s B46 2.0-litre four-cylinder at 255 hp and 294 lb-ft. Its single twin-scroll turbo is paired with direct injection and variable valve control.
This is the rear-wheel-drive 430i two-door Coupé with an eight-speed automatic transmission. The 430i xDrive adds all-wheel drive, while the M440i uses a six-cylinder engine.
Executive comfort powered by a modern turbocharged four.
The G30 530i uses a 2.0-litre turbocharged four-cylinder with direct injection, Valvetronic and Double VANOS. Its US launch ratings are 248 hp and 258 lb-ft.
A straight-six grand tourer with a practical liftback.
The 640i Gran Turismo uses a 3.0-litre turbocharged straight-six rated at 340 PS and 450 Nm. A large tailgate and flexible rear-seat backrest distinguish it from a conventional sedan.
Straight-six refinement in BMW’s flagship sedan.
The sixth-generation 740i uses a 2,998 cm³ turbocharged straight-six. The new engine family combines a twin-scroll turbocharger, direct injection, Valvetronic and Double VANOS.
The G15 M850i combines a 4,395 cm³ N63 V8 with two turbochargers. The US launch specification produces 523 hp and 553 lb-ft in a four-seat grand-touring coupé.
The return of the 8 Series, powered by a 523 hp V8.
A compact X model with a lower, more athletic silhouette.
An eight-speed automatic transmission works with xDrive all-wheel drive. This F39 generation is distinct from the larger U10 X2 and its fully electric iX2 counterpart.
The first-generation X2 xDrive28i has a transversely mounted 2.0-litre turbocharged four-cylinder. Its US specification is rated at 228 hp and 258 lb-ft.
A turbocharged straight-six, an open roof and two seats.
The launch model pairs rear-wheel drive with an eight-speed Sport automatic transmission. Later manual-transmission offerings are separate specifications. The M40i is an M Performance roadster.
The US-market G29 Z4 M40i uses a turbocharged 3.0-litre straight-six rated at 382 hp and 369 lb-ft. European launch output differs from this selected US specification.

The petrol engine alone develops 231 PS and 320 Nm. It drives the rear wheels, while the main electric motor drives the front wheels. A rechargeable battery supplies electric energy. Later 374 PS models have a different battery and system output.

A 2,979 cm³ inline-six with one twin-scroll turbocharger, direct injection and Valvetronic.
The N55’s six cylinders share one crankshaft. In this F10 specification, the engine is mounted longitudinally and sends torque to the rear wheels.

One turbocharger has two exhaust passages feeding its turbine. Exhaust energy spins the compressor, which supplies pressurized intake air. The turbo is largely hidden by surrounding hardware in this reference photograph.
Filtered air enters the compressor, then passes through charge-air cooling before reaching the intake manifold. The intercooler cools the air heated by compression.
S65B40 reference photographed in a 2008 M3 Coupé.
A 3,999 cm³, naturally aspirated V8. Eight individual throttle butterflies and Double VANOS give it a very different character from the turbocharged engines.
The S65 has two banks of four cylinders. BMW quotes 309 kW, equivalent to approximately 420 metric horsepower (PS), and a maximum engine speed of 8,400 rpm.

A larger unit can support more airflow, but its response depends on turbine sizing, engine displacement and control strategy. Bigger does not automatically mean better.
One turbine. One compressor. One shaft.

In a parallel arrangement, separate exhaust groups drive two turbochargers. Their compressors supply the engine’s intake system alongside one another. “Twin-turbo” alone does not tell you whether either turbine housing is single-scroll or twin-scroll.
Two units add plumbing, heat and control complexity. Their response and airflow depend on the complete system, not simply the turbo count.

A divided turbine housing has two scrolls. Carefully grouped cylinders feed separate passages so exhaust pulses interfere less before reaching the turbine. It is a housing design, not a second turbocharger.
It depends on cylinder grouping and a matching divided exhaust manifold. A single-scroll manifold does not become a proper twin-scroll system just by changing the turbo.
Scroll A + Scroll B → one turbine
Change which turbos work as demand rises.

Sequential describes staged operation: one turbo works at low engine demand, then another is introduced as demand increases. Valves manage the transition. The exact routing and activation points depend on the engine.
Staging can widen the useful operating range, but brings extra valves and control complexity. Sequential operation and series compression describe different things and can coexist.
Air leaving one compressor enters a second compressor for another compression stage. This is a series arrangement, unlike two parallel compressors. Bypasses and cooling arrangements vary by design.
Series compression can support a broad operating range and higher pressure ratios. More stages also mean more plumbing, heat management and control requirements.
The air is compressed in two stages.
Adjust the exhaust path through the turbine.
The mechanism must operate in hot exhaust gas. Vane control, durability and material requirements are part of the design, so compatibility cannot be assumed.
An electric motor helps spin the turbo.

An electrically assisted turbo adds a motor to the turbocharger shaft, helping drive the compressor before exhaust energy is sufficient. Some designs can recover energy. This is different from a separate electric compressor or e-booster.
It needs a suitable electrical system, power electronics and thermal management. It is not a plug-in upgrade for every turbocharged BMW.
Count, housing and control are different characteristics. One engine can combine several of these labels. BMW’s “TwinPower Turbo” name does not specify the turbo count.
